Playwright for the mainframe terminal

Panelwright

Drives IBM 3270 applications, TSO, ISPF, CICS, IMS, anything behind a green screen, from the command line, from a real terminal UI, from a VS Code panel, and from AI agents. One daemon holds the session; every surface shares it.

pure TypeScript, zero runtime dependenciesTN3270 / TN3270E direct, TLSvalidated on z/OS, MVS 3.8j (TK5), Galasa SimBankscreenshots below are live captures, nothing mocked

Logging on to TSO on a real MVS system through the CLI. Fields are addressed by the label next to them, not by row and column. The password comes from an environment variable and never touches the command line, the journal or the wire trace. The output after each command is the diff: only the rows that changed.

Vocabulary

3270, in Linux terms

The words get used loosely in every meeting. Pinning them makes the rest of the argument precise.

3270
A family of IBM block-mode terminals from 1971. The host paints a whole screen made of fields, the terminal edits locally, one attention key sends back only the fields that changed. Not a VT100. The nearest Linux thing is an HTML form: the server sends the form, the browser edits it, submit posts the changed inputs.
data stream
The wire format for that screen: orders that position the cursor, start fields, mark them protected or non-display. ANSI escape sequences for addressing, HTML form semantics for fields.
TN3270 / E
The 3270 data stream carried inside telnet. TN3270E adds device type, LU name and response negotiation. Plain, it is unencrypted; enterprises run it over TLS on port 992. The same move Linux made from telnet to SSH around 2000.
emulator
Software pretending to be a 3270. Nobody has a real VT100 either: iTerm2 and Windows Terminal are VT100 emulators. A 3270 emulator is exactly that for z/OS.
TSO, ISPF
TSO is the login shell. ISPF is the full-screen application suite over it. Midnight Commander plus vim plus a menu system.
SDSF, JCL
SDSF is the job and log viewer. JCL is a shell script submitted to a batch queue. top plus journalctl; sbatch.
CICS, IMS
Transaction monitors that own the screen. An application server that also renders its own TUI.
z/OSMF, USS
z/OSMF is the web admin console with a REST API. USS is the POSIX subsystem inside z/OS, and it has real OpenSSH on port 22. Cockpit; and the reason "3270 is the SSH of z/OS" is not quite right.
The need

3270 is the tty of z/OS

SSH is the SSH of z/OS's Unix side. 3270 is the one access path every product, every install guide and every recovery procedure assumes. It is present on day zero of a new LPAR, before z/OSMF, Zowe or any web service is configured. It is closer to the serial console than to a shell: the thing that is there when everything else is broken.

Two properties shape what a good tool for it looks like. SSH is a stream, so its automation tool is expect. 3270 is a screen with fields, so its automation tool is Playwright: locators, a document model, waits for a settled state. And 3270 has no stdout and no exit code, so success is a screen someone has to read. That is a burden for a human and an opportunity for a model, because a structured screen is much closer to a DOM than a byte stream is.

What the Linux world did with its universal path

Where the API shipped in the base image, API-first tooling won: sshd on every distro, the Kubernetes API server, the Docker daemon, the cloud control planes. Where the API was an add-on to install and secure, the universal path won and the API tools ended up riding it.

  • Ansible beat Puppet and Chef by being agentless: it rides SSH instead of inventing an access path. IBM's own Ansible for z/OS runs over SSH into USS, not over z/OSMF.
  • VS Code Remote-SSH hides nothing. It puts the whole IDE on the far end of SSH, and the integrated terminal is one of VS Code's most-used features.
  • Cockpit, Lens, the OpenShift console, Docker Desktop each embed a terminal tab. AWS, Azure and GCP each added a Cloud Shell to their consoles. GitHub added the gh CLI.
  • Windows is the cautionary tale: two decades of MMC-only administration held Windows Server back until PowerShell and Windows Terminal re-embraced the shell.
  • VS Code itself won the editor war this way. It drives the real tools instead of reimplementing them: its terminal is a real shell (xterm.js over your own $SHELL) and it calls the system git binary. Eclipse reimplemented Git in pure Java (JGit and EGit) and treated the terminal as a late, awkward plugin. Developer surveys have put VS Code first, well ahead of Eclipse, for years.

A GUI succeeds as an accelerator for the common case on top of the universal path, never as a replacement for it. What actually replaced typing at SSH was code over the same path: playbooks and Terraform. That is a scripting layer, not a nicer window. The mainframe version of Eclipse's mistake is a Java REST server that must mirror an ISPF application panel by panel, and, like JGit, drifts from the thing it copies. Panelwright is the VS Code choice: drive the real panels.

Why not APIs? A coverage problem, not a pipe dream

z/OSMF REST covers jobs, data sets, USS files and TSO commands, and Zowe is a fine client for it. That is the platform's generic surface. The application surface, Endevor, CA 7, IMS administration, Db2 SPUFI, RACF panels, every vendor ISPF product and fifty years of in-house ISPF applications, is 3270-only, and every enterprise's long tail is different. Each Code4z extension therefore needed its own server-side API, and every one of those is installed through JCL and a 3270 session. Each client feature drags a host-side maintenance action behind it.

Endevor, the concrete case

The gaps between the ISPF dialog and Explorer for Endevor fall into three classes, and only one of them is "the API is missing".

AreaISPF dialogREST v2 / Zowe CLIExplorer for Endevor 1.11.5
Element actionsthe full Quick Edit set: browse, create, edit, changes, signin, generate, delete, master, move, summary, history, listings, components, inputs, outputsadd, update, retrieve, generate, move, transfer, signin, print, delete, queryacm, mergeretrieve, edit, upload, generate, move, delete, sign in and out, history, compare, print listing
Package lifecyclecreate, cast, review, approve, deny, execute, ship, backout, backin, commit, reset, deleteevery one of those is a CLI verbcreate, cast, reset, show SCL. No approve, deny, execute, ship, backout, backin, commit, delete
Batch and SCLoptions 3 and 5 generate SCL from panels, edit, submitsubmit scl for list, element, package, admin, shipnone

API exists, UI never built: the package lifecycle past Cast, a prioritization gap that shows the VS Code teams cannot keep up even where the API is done. API exists only as SCL passthrough: environment administration; the ISPF panels are the friendly form over batch SCL, and rebuilding that form means re-implementing every panel's validation, which is where an "easy" API project turns into months and abends. No API can exist: the User Menu is a standard ISPF panel each site edits with its own CLISTs, and Broadcom's own knowledge base says the primary and environment-selection panels are built dynamically from security checks. Every site's Endevor differs at exactly this layer, and a REST server cannot expose what it does not know about. That last class has one route, and it is the terminal.

"I have my code, my documentation in VS Code, so I expect to have my 3270 emulator there."Customer interview, Code4z 3270 research, 8 participants: 3 sysprogs, 2 DBAs, 3 developers
"I haven't found anything I could run on my new Mac OS device."Same round. Mac and cloud IDE migration is where the search for an emulator starts.

Why do mainframe developers keep an emulator open beside colleagues who write extensions? Because the emulator is the complete surface and every extension is partial. A workflow with one 3270-only step forces it open, and once open it wins by inertia, like the terminal beside every Linux IDE. The extension developers themselves need it to install and configure the backends their extensions talk to, and to verify by eye that the extension did the right thing.

What it is

A Playwright, not an expect

Panelwright was built by using AI to tackle AI use cases: the first job was to let an agent follow a complicated update procedure on a ZD&T system instead of spending unknown days on it by hand. Everything else grew from what that needed.

PlaywrightPanelwright
a browser context that outlives one scripta per-user daemon that holds the TN3270 session, screen buffer, cursor and journal across CLI calls, TUI tabs and VS Code panels
locators: getByLabel, getByRolelocators: after:"Logon ===>", below:"PASSWORD FOR HERC01", rightOf:, last, at:row,col
auto-waiting for a settled pageauto-settle on host quiescence, wait --text READY --last-line, press ENTER --until-gone "***"
trace viewerwire trace decoded in c3270's vocabulary, credentials scrubbed, opened as a structured editor in VS Code
codegenjournal export --script, with redacted writes turned into secret references
Playwright MCP and Playwright CLI for agentsa CLI plus a Claude Code skill; an MCP wrapper is a thin addition when a platform needs one

No API? No problem.

Decades of applications only exist as screens. Panelwright automates them exactly as an operator would: type into fields, press ENTER and PF keys, read what came back.

Built for agents, not just scripts.

One CLI command per action, and after each one a compact, deterministic view of what changed. An agent sees the terminal it is driving without scraping ANSI.

Humans stay in the loop.

A person can watch an agent's session live, take over when a screen needs judgment, and hand control back, all in one shared session. Supervised mode holds every transmit for approval.

Safe by default.

Passwords never reach the command line, the journal or a wire trace. The daemon recognizes password-shaped writes on its own and redacts them however they were typed.

Evidence, not guesswork.

Decoded wire traces, annotations stamped with panel identity, SVG and ANSI screen exports, a privacy-safe diagnostic bundle, and a replayable fake host for hermetic tests.

Real terminal work, done well.

A modern TUI and a native VS Code panel, both with a command palette, autocomplete, find-on-screen, file transfer, 124 host code pages and coaching hints.

Driving ISPF and logging off. Each command is a short-lived process; the daemon keeps the connection between them.

The journal. Every action with the screen fingerprint it saw. The password is redacted at the daemon, not by convention.

Use cases

Four jobs it does today

1. An agent installs and tests software

Every installation guide has at least one mistake, and realistically the most senior engineer on the team is the one who can install the product without help in acceptable time. An agent that follows the guide, hits the mistake and reports it is a product-quality tool before it is a customer tool. KICKS, DOGECICS and a DB2-like SQL engine were installed onto the TK5 image entirely through the Panelwright CLI, and the friction findings became product fixes. Usability testing works the same way: the agent is the first user.

# the agent's own commands, from a real TK5 session
panelwright connect tk5dev
panelwright type after:"Logon ===>" HERC01 --enter
panelwright type below:"PASSWORD FOR HERC01" --secret-env TSO_PW --enter
panelwright press ENTER --until-gone "***"
panelwright wait --text READY --last-line
panelwright type last "ISPF" --enter
panelwright screen                          # compact view: header line + changed rows
panelwright fields --json                   # every writable field, with credentialShaped flags

The skill that teaches an agent all of this installs with panelwright install --skills. From then on, "log on to the mainframe and list my data sets" is a prompt.

2. A human watches, takes over, hands back

panelwright ui --watch attaches a read-only view of the same session with a live activity feed. Press t to take control when a screen needs a person; the agent can ask for exactly that with control request and block until control comes back, or stand by with control listen while a human drives. In supervised mode the agent fills fields and every ENTER waits for an approve or a decline with a comment, in the TUI and in VS Code.

Watching an agent drive ISPF from the TUI. The activity feed on the right names each action and the panel it saw, [panel: ISP@PRIM], because a bundled script recognized it.

3. A current emulator for humans, on a Mac and in a cloud IDE

Everything else feels like Netscape next to Chrome. Auto-size to the window up to ISPF's 160x62 ceiling, field-aware editing with insert and overtype, a command palette, autocomplete per panel and field with one-keystroke password fill from a profile, TSO command history, find on screen, clickable menu options, PF legends and action bars, file transfer, code-page switching mid-session, session tabs, and a coach that names the shortcut you just did the long way. The VS Code panel runs unmodified in code-server, Codespaces and Dev Spaces, because the daemon runs where the extension host runs.

The TUI in manual mode on the ISPF primary option menu, colors from the host's own attributes.

The command palette. Every action and setting, searchable; scripts add their own entries per recognized panel.

The VS Code extension attached to a live session: Sessions and Profiles trees in the sidebar, the OIA strip along the bottom, Zowe team config read as profiles. A Ctrl-click on a data set name opens it in Zowe Explorer; one on a job id opens its spool.

4. Scripts that recognize panels and add commands

A project ships defineSpec modules that recognize application panels, expose commands to the palette, the Scripts view and scripts run, and react to events such as connect or panel:<glob>. Scripts from committed layers are hash-trusted and shown for review before they run. This is the bundled SYSVIEW script, trimmed:

import { defineSpec } from "@panelwright/scripting";

// Anchor on the command line's label, never on position:
// the last unprotected field on a SYSVIEW panel is the scroll amount.
function commandLine(screen) {
  if (screen.row(1).includes("Command ====>")) return { after: "Command" };
  throw new Error("sysview: no command line on this panel");
}

export default defineSpec({
  name: "sysview",
  recognizers: [{ id: "panel", match(screen) { /* GSVX token + dashed title */ } }],
  commands: [{
    id: "sysview-return", title: "SYSVIEW: Return", panel: "*",
    async run(ctx) {
      await ctx.session.type(commandLine(ctx.screen), "RETURN");
      await ctx.session.press("ENTER");
    },
  }],
});

The same mechanism carries the "guidance" idea from the research deck: a recognizer sees ISPF 3.4, the coach offers "Zowe Explorer can browse this" once, and never nags.

Live, in VS Code

Claude Code drives the panel, a human decides

A real Extension Development Host, the real Claude Code extension as the agent, a real TK5 session, recorded on 7 September 2026. The session was opened with supervised: true: Claude fills fields freely, and every ENTER waits for the human's verdict. Chat on the right, the 3270 panel in the middle, the Sessions and Activity trees on the left.

Claude typed the userid and pressed ENTER with a reason. The proposal docks below the screen; the typed field and the cursor are marked on the screen itself. Approve or Decline.

The password proposal shows provenance, never the value. The card reads <secret, 6 chars, declared> and the journal entry says <redacted>. The value came from the profile's secret source and reached neither the card nor the chat.

A decline steers the agent. The human declined LISTC LEVEL(HERC04) with the comment "use LISTC LEVEL(HERC03) instead". Claude received it as exit code 20 with the comment verbatim, and asked before re-proposing the corrected command.

The same session also supports the other direction of handoff: Claude drives to a screen it should not fill, asks for control with a reason, the human takes the panel, types, and grants control back, and Claude's blocked request returns with the answer. Both flows were found and fixed by running the real agent against the real host before either shipped.

Integrations

Where it plugs into Code4z

Nothing in Code4z has a session or host concept beyond the Zowe profile, so the integration currency is the profile, Zowe's URI schemes and commands, and the one Broadcom-to-Broadcom API that exists. All of it was measured from the shipped bundles.

Already built, in to out

Data set names on the screen open in Zowe Explorer through zowe.ds.setDataSetFilter. Job ids open their spool. Members opened through zowe-ds: URIs get COBOL and HLASM language support attached for free.

Found in the bundles

Zowe Explorer registers, but does not contribute, zowe.jobs.setJobSpool(profile, jobId), a job reveal Broadcom's own debugger calls. Explorer for Endevor exports listElements, getElement, listMembers, isEndevorElement and friends, consumed by HLASM and COBOL Language Support.

Next, in to out

An Endevor element list on a panel offers "open in Explorer for Endevor" through that exported API. A tn3270 Zowe profile type puts sessions wherever Code4z lists connections and borrows credentials the way the debugger does.

Next, out to in

"Run in ISPF" from Explorer for Endevor for the steps it lacks: approve, execute, ship, environment admin, the User Menu. "Open SDSF at this job" from a failed job. The extension publishes an action API the Code4z way, through getExtension().exports.

A precedent inside the portfolio. HB.js for VS Code already ships a 3270 screen canvas inside a webview, fed by the HostBridge server, CICS-only, to record green-screen flows and generate test APIs. Broadcom has already decided a 3270 surface belongs in VS Code, for one product.

The realistic shape for Endevor is a hybrid, not a replacement. Explorer for Endevor keeps the tree and the editor. A bridge opens the emulator already positioned on the right panel with the element or package filled in, driven by a script that a site can adjust without a release. The reverse direction works through the API Endevor already exports. The cost is one TSO session per developer, which they hold anyway, and one profile setting naming the site's Endevor entry path.

The VS Code command palette filtered to Panelwright. Every contributed command is also callable by another extension.

Business case

The currency is usage

The reviewer's note on the research deck is right: packaging and application switching are not problems clients will pay for. The deck already answers it by moving to integrations, guidance and AI. Three things are worth paying for.

  • The emulator is a distribution channel, not a product. VS Code is free and sells Azure. Playwright is free and is a moat. A free, current emulator keeps a Mac developer or a cloud-IDE developer on the platform, and every retained developer is licensed-product usage.
  • The AI angle is where new budget exists. Playwright CLI and Playwright MCP are how agents drive browsers. Panelwright is that for 3270, and no competitor ships an agent-driven emulator inside VS Code. Rocket BlueZone Web and OpenText Host Access for the Cloud are browser emulators, not agent surfaces.
  • Install testing is a product-quality tool first. An agent that follows an install guide and reports the mistake should run on Broadcom's own documentation before it ships. That is a cost already paid in senior-engineer time.

A structure that reconciles open and closed: the emulator core and the agent CLI open source, ideally contributed to Zowe so Broadcom holds the position Microsoft holds with Playwright, with the Code4z integrations, guidance packs and dedicated agents as the paid value on top.

Try it

Ten minutes to a live session

Today it builds from a checkout. Once published to npm and the Marketplace, the first three lines become npm install -g @panelwright/cli and the extension installs from VS Code like any other.

git clone <repo> && cd panelwright
npm install && npm run build
npm run cli:link                    # puts panelwright on your PATH
                                    # after publish: npm install -g @panelwright/cli

panelwright connect mainframe.example.com:23
panelwright screen
panelwright ui --watch              # in a second terminal

npm run vsix                        # builds the VS Code extension, CLI bundled inside
code --install-extension dist-pack/panelwright-*.vsix
